#4329. Tesla FSD v15 is AI4’s last shot as Musk reveals how little compute is left

Tesla’s FSD v15 is its last real shot at delivering unsupervised self-driving on the AI4 computer in millions of customer cars. Elon Musk spent the weekend explaining on X how the new software uses the hardware, and there isn’t much room left.

He also confirmed that cars won’t get the next-gen AI5 chip, and that the mid-cycle AI4.5 upgrade just had its RAM cut from 32GB to 24GB.

The most visible part of FSD v15 is Tesla Reality View, a live, video-game-like rendering of the car’s surroundings with chevrons floating in the sky for upcoming turns. Musk called it “real-time AI video generation (no gaming engine!) using just half of one AI4 TRIP accelerator.”

The fan accounts ran with that as a flex. But Musk’s follow-up posts tell a different story.

He explained that after Tesla moved a decoder into SRAM, “we only have half a TRIP out of three on SoC B, for this reality visualizer, so spent the compute as best we could.” In other words, half a TRIP is what was left over. He added that TRIP, Tesla’s neural accelerator, “basically only handles 8-bit int and has to run softmax in emulation mode in 28 steps.”

In another post, Musk described Reality View as a roughly 1-billion-parameter diffusion model running off the same vision encoder features “that are plugged into the 3B encoder model that produces the driving actions.” He admitted the visualization’s latency is “a bit high due to compute constraints.”

That 3B figure is worth noting. Tesla talked up a 10x jump in FSD model size for over a year, first for v14 and then for v15. Musk didn’t say whether 3B covers the entire driving stack, but it’s nowhere near 10x.

And Tesla’s own engineers aren’t describing a chip with lots of headroom. Dilreet Raju, who works on Tesla’s AI silicon, wrote that the hardest work of his life was co-designing the v15 vision encoder “to squeeze out the last few percents of MFU from AI4.” MFU is model FLOPs utilization, a measure of how much of the chip’s theoretical compute the model actually uses. Musk replied with a target emoji.

When Tesla unveiled its FSD computer in 2019, the selling point was redundancy: two independent chips on one board, each with its own power and memory, so one could take over if the other failed. As we noted when Tesla started shipping the AI4.5 computer in Model Y in January, Tesla’s FSD computers have historically used two identical chips for exactly that reason.

That’s what an unsupervised, Level 4 system needs. With nobody in the driver’s seat, a hardware fault can’t simply hand control back to a human. The car needs enough healthy compute left to keep seeing the road and pull over safely.

But Musk’s own description shows SoC B running the decoder and the Reality View model, not sitting idle as a mirror of SoC A. Tesla hackers, including greentheonly, have reported for years that Tesla started splitting its FSD workload across both chips back in the HW3 days.

Tesla has never explained how much of AI4 it reserves for failover, or whether a single SoC can run enough of the stack to bring a car to a safe stop on its own. The more of the board v15 needs, the harder that question gets.

Waymo has answered it publicly. The company says both of its onboard computing systems run full workloads in parallel and that a secondary computer can bring the vehicle to a safe stop if the primary fails, backed by redundant braking, steering and power. Its new custom chip is rated at more than 1,000 TOPS. By our own comparison of AI4 and Nvidia’s Drive Thor, AI4 is estimated at roughly 100 to 150 TOPS across both chips.

Tesla started rolling out FSD v15 on Saturday, claiming “25x better handling of safety critical cases” without any baseline. So far, the people posting videos are mostly the usual crowd of Tesla-focused accounts that get early builds. Just hours before the rollout started, Musk wrote that v15 “goes to wide release next month.”

The early clips are almost all about Reality View, the new parking spot selection, and the floating arrows. Those are UI features. They say very little about how many miles v15 can drive between critical interventions, which is the only number that matters for unsupervised driving.

That brings us to AI4.5. On Tesla’s Q1 2026 earnings call, Musk announced an “AI4 Plus” with RAM doubled from 16GB to 32GB per chip, which raised the question of whether HW4 would follow HW3.

This weekend, Musk said “AI4.5 is a relatively small performance improvement that is mostly due to needing to upgrade RAM to LPDDR5X.” Hours later, he added: “RAM is super expensive, so we reduced AI4.5 from 32GB to 24GB. That will be fine. It’s hard to use 32GB anyway, given memory bandwidth constraints.”

He also said that AI4 “costs twice as much now due to memory and storage price hikes.”

So the mid-cycle refresh exists mainly because Tesla needs a newer memory type it can actually buy, not to unlock bigger models. If memory bandwidth is the bottleneck, as Musk keeps repeating, adding capacity doesn’t change much.

Asked by an owner on Sunday whether to wait for AI5 before upgrading from HW3, Musk answered: “It’s going to Optimus. Cars will remain at AI4. That’s enough to solve superhuman driving.”

An interesting comment, as it destroys one thing that HW3 owners were holding to: Tesla was delaying HW3 upgrades until it had AI5. Now, it’s clearly not the case and Tesla has no excuse not to upgrade HW3 cars.

He described AI5 as “a gigantic improvement. Roughly 12X more compute,” and later as “roughly an order of magnitude hardware performance improvement, all things considered. Memory bandwidth is a constraint.” Last year, he said that by some metrics AI5 would be 40 times better than AI4.

AI5 is also moving around. In October, Musk said Tesla cut AI5’s RAM in half to 72GB to get enough volume for Optimus, then nudged it back up to 96GB a day later. AI6 was cut by a third, to 144GB of LPDDR6. When asked about AI6 this weekend, Musk replied with a chef’s kiss meme.

As we reported in July, Samsung’s Texas fab won’t reach AI5 volume production until the second half of 2027, nearly two years behind Musk’s original timeline. And that volume is now headed to robots and data centers, not cars.

This is the situation for AI4 owners: v15 has to be the one. And we heard Elon Musk calling every FSD update “the one” for the last decade.

Tesla’s own engineers are talking about squeezing the last few percent of utilization out of AI4. Musk describes a half-accelerator scrap of compute left for the visualizer. The AI4.5 refresh is a RAM swap that just got downsized, and AI5 isn’t coming to cars. If v15 can’t get to unsupervised driving on AI4, there’s no hardware escape hatch for the fleet.

I seem to remember a couple of years ago Tesla released a big update in November, only to encounter chip overheating problems the following summer. Now they are admitting that the old chip is running flat out, that means heat. Heat that they have to get rid of in cars that already are dealing with inadequate cooling.

We’ve seen this movie before. Tesla said HW3 was enough for unsupervised self-driving until it wasn’t, and those owners are still waiting on an answer about upgrades. AI4 owners paid for the same promise.

And even if v15 drives well, I want to know how Tesla handles a chip failure with nobody behind the wheel. That’s not optional for Level 4. If the stack needs both SoCs to drive, what brings the car to a safe stop when one of them crashes?

As for v15 itself, I’m not drawing conclusions from influencer clips. Reality View looks great, but it’s also visibly laggy, and Musk admits it’s compute-limited. A great visual update is nice. Driving performance is what matters. I’ll wait until I get it in my own car to see how big the improvement actually is.

#4328. Carnegie Mellon’s Buggy Is the 100-Year-Old Race Series You Never Knew About, But Won’t Be Able to Stop Watching

Race pits teams against each other to engineer a new vehicle every year that balances aero, handling, and weight, while enabling a driver to somehow squeeze inside.

Ever heard of Buggy? With a capital B? Referring to a specific type of racing? Neither had we, until recently—but where there’s racing, count Road & Track intrigued. Buggy, so you know, is a unique form of racing only taking place at Carnegie Mellon University (CMU), and it’s been happening for more than 100 years. Similar to Formula SAE, students engineer, build, and drive the vehicles that compete in the odd spectacle. And yes, in case you were questioning how the buggy is driven, someone is actually inside that tube of carbon fiber.

To understand how this sport works from the car design to the track, Road & Track spoke with Caroline Kiesnowski, the head mechanic and driver for a team. Currently a junior in mechanical engineering at CMU, she broke down what it takes to compete in Buggy.

“Basically, the easiest way to describe it is you put a person in a tube, and you use it as a baton in a relay race,” Kiesnowski says. “You get pushed up two hills, you do a free roll where the driver is completely in control—they're steering and everything—and then you get pushed back up three more hills to a finish line.”

It’s incredibly competitive, with lots of teams vying for the win. Just like professional motorsports, each team designs a new buggy every year using experience from years past and new digital tools to refine the vehicle. The priorities are fairly self explanatory: you want the smallest, lightest buggy possible for being pushed up the hill, then for the downhill sections, designing a buggy with the smallest coefficient of drag and wheels with minimal rolling resistance is paramount. Speeds top out around 40 miles per hour, so these little vehicles are positively cruising at their fastest pace—especially considering their pilots are a foot above the pavement.

The students who end up piloting them are highly recruited, Kiesnowski tells me. Each team wants the smallest possible buggy, which means you need a small person to design the buggy’s body around. If you watch how a driver load into their respective buggy, you’ll quickly understand how tight the squeeze is and how much the design is centered around the driver.

While most of the course is straight or mild curves, there’s one rather challenging turn called The Chute. It’s the source of many crashes and spins, and is something students need to design their buggy around every year. Two layouts are widely used: one is the standard trike that positions two wheels in the rear and one in the front; while the other is the reverse trike, which, logically, puts two wheels up front and one in the rear.

They each have their pros and cons, but in general, the standard trike is thought to be a bit dodgier in The Chute. With only one front wheel controlling steering and turning, it’s a simple design, but ergonomics and visibility for the driver can suffer. Meanwhile, the reverse trikes most often use Ackermann-style steering, which increases complexity, but Kiesnowski finds it to be a better design for steering and braking.

“The steering question is interesting because of the nature of buggy,” Kiesnowski said. “It's in a sense, proprietary information; it's historically been super-secret about people talking about their teams. Some teams even have blacked out windshields, like reflective windshields, so you can't see their steering.”

Another challenge for the track is that said track is actually just a road, and it’s mighty bumpy. Kiesnowski recalls that teams in the past even designed suspension to give the trike a better ride, but it’s a rare design choice that adds weight to a structure you’re trying to keep as light as possible. And yes, there is passing, especially in the downhill roll section, so you could end up doing some proper wheel-to-wheel racing. As you’d expect, though, safety is the number one goal in this whole competition, so drivers have helmets, and there are regulations teams have to follow in building their vehicles to ensure the sport is as safe as possible.

As with any good motorsports event, I asked Kiesnowski about teams trying to bend the rules and regulations for an advantage. She declined to offer details, but still said there have indeed been instances of teams looking for an advantage beyond the book. (After all, the grand prize of pride and bragging rights over your peers is a mighty tempting trophy in college.)

The competition takes place every April at Carnegie Mellon’s campus in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. And while the engines are essentially members of the team pushing, it’s still a form of racing we can get excited about.

#4327. BYD Barred from Selling Ti7 SUV in EU Because of a Copycat Design

A Dutch court barred BYD from selling the SUV in the European Union, ruling that the company copied the design of the Land Rover Defender too closely.

A Dutch court has ruled that BYD cannot sell the Ti7 mid-size three-row SUV in the European Union, according to a report from Automotive News. According to the report, a preliminary ruling from the Dutch court found BYD guilty of copyright infringement, with the Ti7 ruled to be a dupe of the Land Rover Defender.

Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) brought the case against BYD earlier this year after the Chinese automaker announced that it would launch the car in the United Kingdom in 2027. The preliminary ruling marks a significant setback in BYD’s recent explosive expansion into Europe.

See all results for used cars for sale near 78130

“In these summary proceedings, the preliminary relief judge rules that the Ti7 infringes the EU design of Jaguar Land Rover,” the court said in its November 20 ruling, AN reported. “The characteristic and distinctive elements of the design are reflected in the BYD Ti7.”

The Defender is JLR’s best-selling vehicle globally, with the automaker shipping more than 100,000 units last year. Both vehicles have boxy designs with flat rooflights, squared wheel arches, and, notably, body-colored panels in place of the rear side windows.

Unfortunately for JLR, the judge also ruled that the court does not have authority over BYD’s U.K. arm. To that end, JLR is reportedly planning to bring the same claim to the courts in England.

According to AN, BYD “strongly disagrees” with the ruling and has plans to appeal the result. “The BYD Ti7 is the result of BYD’s own independent design work and infringes none of JLR’s rights,” the company said. “We will pursue every legal avenue to demonstrate that this decision is incorrect.”

While the final ruling will likely take some time before it is announced, the Dutch court has prohibited BYD from producing the Ti7 at its new factory in Hungary, where it was due to begin mass production early next year.

#4326. Toyota is giving the Corolla a radical makeover, including its first 100% electric version

Toyota is overhauling its best-selling vehicle of all time, which will include the first fully electric Corolla.

The Toyota Corolla is one of the most recognized and best-selling automotive nameplates of all time.

Since its debut in 1966, over 57 million drivers have chosen the Corolla thanks to its reliability, low cost of ownership, efficiency, and affordable price tag.

Toyota sells the Corolla in more than 150 countries and has expanded the lineup over the past 50 years from sedans and hatchbacks to coupes, wagons, a sporty GR Corolla, and the Corolla Cross compact SUV.

For its 13th generation, Toyota is planning a major overhaul that’s expected to be its biggest transformation yet.

The next-gen Toyota Corolla will be based on a new “multipathway” platform that will support gas, hybrid, plug-in hybrid, and, for the first time, fully electric powertrains.

“Whether it’s a battery EV, plug-in hybrid, hybrid, or internal combustion engine vehicle ― whatever the power source ― let’s make good-looking cars that everyone will want to drive!” Toyota’s former president and current CEO Koji Sato said after unveiling the Corolla Concept at the Japan Mobility Show last October.

Toyota has kept most details a secret, including battery and powertrain specs. However, the new version is expected to adopt a similar design to the concept.

“When we created the concept, we wanted to give the Corolla name a new twist,” Norihiko Kobayashi, who has led the Corolla program since 2011, told Motor.es during a recent interview.

The Corolla has undergone several minor updates over the past 60 years, but the next-gen model will look nothing like its predecessors.

“It wasn’t simply about following in the footsteps of the past,” Kobayashi explained, “we wanted to delve into the future while still maintaining the Corolla identity.”

Developing the next-gen Corolla “wasn’t just about making a new car, but about redefining the future without looking back,” he added.

Like the current version, the new Toyota Corolla will come in several different body types, including a sedan, hatchback, crossover, and a GR variant.

If they can deliver a Corolla cross EV for $30k sticker that dealers sell for $27k. That could be a large market a win for everyone . They appear to be doing what they did with hybrid and what KHG did with some models for a few years. Just starting with hybrid then going shades to pure bev.

Details have yet to be confirmed, but the Toyota Corolla EV is expected to be available in single- and dual-motor configurations and offer a pure electric driving range of at least 250 miles.

The hybrid will reportedly use a new 1.5-liter four-cylinder engine and an electric motor. Toyota’s engineers told Car and Driver the hybrid system would deliver around 134 horsepower. It’s also estimated to be 10% to 20% more efficient than the current Corolla.

Toyota’s next-gen Corolla is expected to debut sometime in 2027 as a 2028 model year. According to Car and Driver, the gas version will likely start at around $25,000, the hybrid around $27,000, and the EV and PHEVs will likely be priced in the $30,000 range.

#4325. Hyundai Ioniq 5 Maintenance Guide: What Needs Servicing And What Doesn’t

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

It’s no secret that electric cars are more affordable to maintain than their gasoline-powered counterparts. While they may have a higher purchase price than a comparable gas-powered vehicle, EVs can save owners money over time by eliminating the need for regular engine oil changes, emissions tests, and other traditional maintenance tasks. Affordable electric vehicles are also becoming increasingly common, with even more options expected to arrive in the coming years.

However, that doesn't mean electric cars are completely maintenance-free. Like any other vehicle, EVs require regular care and attention to remain reliable and perform at their best for many years.

Although they don't have conventional combustion engines or traditional automatic transmissions, electric cars still feature components that require periodic maintenance. These include reduction gearboxes, brake fluid, brake pads, coolant systems, and tires among other things. Keeping these components in good condition is essential to ensuring an EV's long-term reliability.

ERANGE EV tires are purpose-built for electric vehicles, combining efficiency, comfort and performance with advanced EcoPoint3 technology.

For the second installment of our EV maintenance series, I'll be taking a closer look at the Hyundai Ioniq 5, one of the most recognizable electric crossovers on the market. Made in the United States and South Korea, the Ioniq 5 has long been one of the biggest rivals to the ubiquitous Tesla Model Y.

I'll break down Hyundai's recommended maintenance schedule, explaining which items are required to keep the vehicle running smoothly over the long term.

Compared to Tesla, which is known for its rather skimpy maintenance plan, Hyundai includes a generous list of maintenance items in the owner’s manual. The automaker also includes additional service actions that should be performed if the car is used in harsher-than-normal conditions, so owners know what to expect in the long run.

There’s a normal maintenance schedule and a separate section for severe usage and low mileage conditions. Hyundai also has a list of maintenance items that can be performed by the owner. I’ll go through all of them, so drivers can easily mark down what needs to be done during the car’s lifetime.

Hyundai says that normal driving conditions include distances longer than 10 miles, clean roads without salt or dust, ambient temperatures under 90ºF (32ºC), no towing, no roof rack, and normal speeds. Under these conditions, the required maintenance for a Hyundai Ioniq 5 is as follows, according to the owner’s manual:

According to Hyundai, extra precaution needs to be taken if the car is driven under certain conditions. These include repeated driving short distances of less than five miles in normal temperatures or less than 10 miles in freezing temperatures, and driving on rough, dusty, muddy, unpaved, graveled, or salt-spread roads.

But that’s not all. Driving in areas using salt or other corrosive materials, or in very cold weather, driving in heavy dust conditions, driving in heavy traffic areas with the ambient temperature higher than 90ºF (32 ºC) while consuming more than 50% of electric energy, and driving on uphill, downhill, or mountain roads repeatedly can also result in extra maintenance items.

Towing a trailer, using a roof rack, driving as a patrol car or taxi, frequently driving at high speeds, and frequently driving in stop-and-go conditions are also part of the conditions that lead to more intense servicing requirements.

In addition to the normal maintenance schedule above, Hyundai recommends the following actions for severe usage and low-mileage conditions:

All of these items should be performed by a Hyundai technician, but the Ioniq 5 also has a consistent list of maintenance actions that should be performed by the owner.

The Hyundai Ioniq 5 is one of the best-selling electric crossovers in the United States, and for good reason. Its unique styling has plenty of fans, and it’s a genuinely nice car to drive. As for its maintenance requirements, the official recommendations have a lot more items compared to the Tesla Model Y, but at the end of the day, most of them are just inspection jobs. As a result, maintenance costs should be quite low compared to a comparable gas vehicle. Just rotate and replace tires, keep an eye on your brakes, and swap out the coolant after 10 years or 120,000 miles.

#4324. BYD Ti7 banned from the EU for copying the Land Rover Defender’s design

A Dutch court has barred BYD from selling or building its Ti7 SUV anywhere in the European Union after ruling that it infringes Jaguar Land Rover’s registered design for the Land Rover Defender. Breaking the injunction costs BYD €100,000 per day, up to €10 million.

It’s a sharp turnaround from 10 days ago, when the same court in The Hague handed BYD an early win in the Defender copycat fight. BYD’s Hong Kong shares fell as much as 4% on Monday before closing 1.9% lower.

The preliminary relief judge at the District Court of The Hague issued the ruling on Friday, November 20, in summary proceedings JLR brought against 11 BYD companies.

JLR put six registered EU designs in front of the court. The judge only needed one of them: design 005248580-0004, registered in April 2018 and covering the current Defender 110, known internally as the L663.

According to the ruling, the elements that dominate that design are the rounded “shoulders,” the rounded corners, the signature panel on the C-pillar, the rounded wheel-arch cutouts, the continuous window line, and the overall silhouette. The court found every one of them on the Ti7.

Here’s how the two SUVs compare from the same angles, using official press images from BYD and JLR:

BYD argued that the headlights, grille, bumpers, hood and side profile are all different. Not enough, said the judge, who ruled that those differences, on their own or combined, don’t give an informed user a different overall impression. The court also found the Ti7 sits closer to the Defender than to older boxy SUVs like the Ford Flex, Jeep Wrangler and Mercedes G-Class.

BYD doesn’t sell the Ti7 in the EU. It told the court it has “no concrete plans” to launch it there and that the SUV can only be ordered in the UK.

The judge didn’t buy that as a defense. By BYD’s own account, it developed the seven-seat layout for the UK and Europe, a promotional video called the Ti7 the first seven-seat SUV “in Europe,” and BYD wouldn’t commit to keeping it out of the EU. That was enough for the court to find a threat of infringement.

So BYD’s EU entities can no longer import, produce, offer, sell, store or supply the Ti7. The order kicks in one week after the ruling is formally served, and it even covers BYD’s Hungarian unit, since the judge considered it conceivable the Ti7 could come out of the new Szeged factory.

The UK is a different story. The court said it has no jurisdiction over BYD UK and threw out JLR’s UK design claims, so British deliveries are still on for January 2027. That’s the one European market where BYD actually opened orders, pricing the Ti7 at £47,995, about £24,000 below the £71,840 plug-in Defender 110.

BYD said it “strongly disagrees” with the judgment and will appeal, adding that the Ti7 “is the result of BYD’s own independent design work and infringes none of JLR’s rights.” JLR told AFP it protects its intellectual property and takes legal action when necessary.

BYD has four weeks to appeal, but the injunction stays in force while it does. JLR, for its part, has six months to file a full case on the merits, or BYD can get the injunction lifted.

There’s more coming. JLR also has a separate case in Rotterdam over copyright and “slavish imitation,” with a hearing scheduled for Wednesday.

This whole thing started in August, when JLR had bailiffs raid BYD’s Dutch offices in Schiedam and Hoofddorp. The court later ordered JLR to destroy everything it seized, saying it didn’t need BYD’s internal files to make its design case. And it didn’t. JLR won on the design registration alone.

The Ti7 looks like a Defender. We said so when BYD first brought it to the UK, and so did pretty much everyone else. Chinese automakers have been building Defender lookalikes for years, but most of them stayed in China.

BYD brought one to the Defender’s home turf at a £24,000 discount, so a fight with JLR was always coming.

"...ruled that those differences, on their own or combined, don’t give an informed user a different overall impression."

Really? I feel like anyone who pays even a little attention to car designs isn't going to mistake the two. The thing most people see as differentiating within the same category is the headlights, tail lights, grill - which are all significantly different.

The only real similarity is the proportions, there are a ton of similarly proportioned SUVs but that's a result of the form factor.

But honestly, all these boxy SUVs look the same to me.

Nobody owns “boxy.” JLR even failed to trademark the classic Defender’s shape in the UK, a fight it lost in its legal battle with the Ineos Grenadier. But it registered the new Defender’s design in 2018, and that specific combination of shoulders, C-pillar panel and wheel arches is exactly what the court protected. That’s how design rights are supposed to work.

The actual business damage is small for now. The Ti7 sells roughly 30,000 units a month, almost all in China, and the UK launch goes ahead. The stock dip was about headlines more than lost Ti7 sales.

#4323. Lucid Gravity Robotaxis Begin Driverless Testing for Future Uber Service

A collaboration between Lucid, Uber, and Nuro enters the next testing stage, ditching the human safety net for test drives in the San Francisco Bay Area.

The San Francisco Bay Area has become an unofficial proving ground for robotaxis, with companies like Waymo, Zoox, and Tesla running supervised road tests on San Francisco’s streets. A fleet of specially equipped Lucid Gravity SUVs has also been on the prowl in the Bay Area this year, testing a self-driving ride-hailing experience for Uber. While these tests have been run with a safety driver ready to take over, the Gravity SUVs are now going fully driverless.

The modified Gravity SUVs are the product of a collaboration between Lucid, Uber, and Nuro, a company that builds autonomous driving software. The robotaxis feature an Uber-designed cabin interface and are operated by Nuro’s autonomous driving system. High-resolution cameras, lidar sensors, and radar sensors are integrated into the Gravity’s body and mounted to a rooftop “halo” that doubles as a way for riders to identify the correct vehicle through LED lights.

See all results for new 2027 Lucid Motors Gravity for sale near 21014

Testing first began with human supervision in the Bay Area in December 2025. Since then, Nuro has continued to conduct supervised round-the-clock testing in San Francisco and Houston. The company now says it’s ready to begin its next phase, which involves driving on public roads without a safety operator inside.

Lucid built and delivered over 100 autonomous vehicles to complete this next stage. The California Department of Motor Vehicles has issued two permits this year that allow the vehicles to test on public roads without a safety operator inside and allow for passenger rides when a safety driver is present.

As part of the collaboration’s terms, Uber has committed to owning and operating at least 35,000 Lucid vehicles equipped with Nuro’s autonomous technology. The service is expected to launch to the public in the Bay Area by early 2027, followed by launches in dozens of global markets over the next few years.

Elon loves to mash his companies together. He claims the Roadster has boosters from SpaceX, and the Cybercab has Starlink internet. And its coming to more Teslas, Musk said Monday. He claimed it will be available on all Tesla models by the end of 2027, though I don't put too much stake in his timelines generally.

This came in response to X user David Marcus, who said: "Can't wait for Tesla to offer an embedded Starlink option on all models (beyond the Cybercab)."

"Hopefully available toward the end of next year," he said in the X reply. "This will be important for unsupervised FSD, so passengers have high bandwidth everywhere for work and entertainment."

He did add a single caveat, though. "Except in China, as Starlink is illegal there."

It will be interesting to see how Tesla physically integrates Starlink into the back of other Tesla models, though. The Cybercab has its antennae panel built into the roof, and you can see its little square cutout. However, that would require redesigning the roof panels of all existing Tesla models, which isn't exactly easy. Unless owners would be cool with an additional panel being mounted on top of the car, like the big flat antennae we saw being tested on the Cybertruck recently.

However, according to Tesla's AI lead Ashok Elluswamy, Cybercab passengers currently can't connect to Starlink, as it's only used for fleet management, navigation, and customer service. Elon's timelines are about as reliable as mine when I tell my wife I'm gonna mow the lawn on Football Sunday. However, the technology already seems like it's there with the Cybercab, and the patent is already filed. It's just a matter of integrating it into existing models.

#4320. This Little Electric Truck Looks Like France's Answer To The Slate

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Slate made a big splash with its affordable, heavily customizable electric truck. Someone even copied the formula over to a lineup of gas-powered trucks, and we'll see another cheap electric truck from Ford next year. But now the French have their own cheap electric truck concept. It's called the Kilow La Bagnole (which literally translates to "the car"), and it's adorable. I need one.

The La Bagnole is one of the most interesting looking cars I've ever seen, It looks like a French Willy's Jeep but with the fully open wheels of F1 car. It only seats two and two different kinds of body styles, Hard Top (basically a pickup truck) and Closed Hard Top (becomes a van). Both can be had with roof bars so you can put all sorts of gear up there. If you get the Hard Top, the side bed rails are made from either resin-bonded wood fiber or Okoume wood. The former makes it look like it's from IKEA, while the latter looks more premium. However, the Okoume wood requires periodic to keep it weather proof.

Both versions come with an optional removable roof, which is pretty awesome. So you can have either a targa-top pickup or van. The standard La Bagnole lacks doors, and only has big metal side bars, but you can option transparent doors, which are neat.

If you want colors, boy can you get 'em. Kilow offers 12 different regular color options, six gradient colors, and six sparkly "Memories" colors. The best part is that they're all free options. The chassis of the La Bagnole is steel, but all of its body panels are easy removable. So if one breaks or dents, you can just replace it.

There are a few different battery options. Two of the options are made to allow unlicensed drivers to use them. Both the 6 kWh and 12 kWh "Long Range" batteries require no license, as they're classified as quadricycles and capped at 45 km/h (28 mph). Trucks with the 6 kWh battery have only 70 km (43 miles) of range. Cars with the 12 kWh battery can go 164 km (102 miles). The third option mates the 12 kWh battery with an increased speed limiter of 80 km/h (50 mph), but that requires a driver's license.

I love this little thing, and I wish it was coming to the United States. As of right now, it will only be offered in Europe, starting in France. The La Bagnole is such a charming, fun looking little utility vehicle that seems designed equally for function and form. With prices ranging from €10,800 ($11,758) - €13,690 ($14,904), it's an affordable work vehicle for anyone who needs one and stays local, but with tons of character.

#4319. Subaru is cutting EV prices by dropping one of its most distinctive features

Subaru vehicles are known for their dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) capabilities, but to cut costs, the company is now offering front-wheel-drive (FWD) versions on select electric models.

The Uncharted EV went on sale earlier this year as a smaller, sportier entry-level electric crossover positioned below the Solterra.

It was also the first Subaru model in about 30 years not to come with standard all-wheel drive. After unveiling the Uncharted EV last summer, Subaru said, “For buyers focused on affordability and range, the entry-level Uncharted Premium FWD model will be offered in limited numbers.”

Apparently, it wasn’t too limited. The 2027 Uncharted EV is now on sale, still with the base Premium FWD model equipped with a single 221-horsepower front-mounted electric motor.

Higher-priced Uncharted trims, including the Sport and GT, are upgraded with Subaru’s Symmetrical All-Wheel Drive system with X-Mode, delivering a combined 338 horsepower.

The 2027 Subaru Uncharted EV Premium FWD starts at $34,995, while the Sport and GT are priced from $39,795 and $43,795, respectively.

In the US, the 2027 Solterra and larger Trailseeker are still equipped with standard AWD, but Subaru is introducing new FWD (4×2) variants in some markets at a lower price point.

In comparison, the 2027 Subaru Solterra and Trailseeker EV start at $38,495 and $39,995, respectively.

Subaru opened preorders for its new 2027 electric range in Spain, including the Unchartered, Solterra, and E-Outback, which is sold as the Trailseeker in the US.

All of which will be available with a lower-priced FWD variant. Like the Uncharted, Subaru will still offer AWD on higher-priced Solterra and E-Outback trims.

The new Subaru Uncharted (4×2) starts at €26,525 ($28,900), the Solterra (4×2) starts at €35,025 ($38,200), and the E-Outback (4×2) starts at €36,525 ($39,800) in Spain, including subsidies, discounts, and other incentives.

Preorders are open for the Uncharted, while the Solterra and E-Outback are expected to launch in mid-2027.

Will Subaru expand FWD (4×2) to other vehicles and markets, like the US? The Uncharted is still Subaru’s only EV sold with standard FWD. The 2027 Solterra and Trailseeker are equipped with AWD and X-Mode.

For a small electric car driven on pavement I prefer RWD, which offers less complexity, better uphill traction, and a tighter turning circle. I love the handling of my last two cars, a RWD Miata and a RWD BMW i3 (old style).

Subaru is already selling considerably more EVs in the US, with three affordable, practical electric SUVs: the Uncharted, Solterra, and Trailseeker.

In Spring 2027, it will add its first three-row electric SUV, the Getaway. It wouldn’t be a surprise to see Subaru introduce a FWD option for other models, like the Solterra, at a lower price point.

Then again, AWD is used significantly more in the US than in Spain and other markets. For now, the Uncharted remains Subaru’s sole FWD model.

#4317. A decades-old mystery about light could hold the key to faster internet

Light can carry vast amounts of information, but developing faster and more efficient optical communication systems requires precise control over how it travels. Scientists have now made an important advance in understanding barium titanate (BTO), a promising material that could help improve the performance of future devices that transmit information using light.

A research team led by KAIST has uncovered detailed information about how light moves through BTO and how much of it the material absorbs. These properties have been difficult to measure accurately for decades because of the crystal's complicated internal structure. The new findings provide engineers with a more reliable foundation for designing optical devices that minimize signal loss and support faster data transmission.

KAIST (President Choongsik Bae) announced the results on November 8. The research was led by Professor Min Seok Jang of KAIST's School of Electrical Engineering, working with Professor Harry A. Atwater's group at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), the Korea Research Institute of Standards and Science (KRISS), and U.S.-based J.A. Woollam Co. Together, the researchers examined how BTO interacts with light across wavelengths extending from the ultraviolet to the far-infrared.

Why Barium Titanate Could Transform Optical Communications

One of BTO's most valuable characteristics is its ability to change how it affects light when electricity is applied. This behavior, called the Pockels effect, gives the material a strong electro-optic response and makes it especially attractive for optical modulators. These components convert electrical information into signals carried by light, making them important building blocks for advanced communication systems.

However, producing reliable devices requires a detailed understanding of two fundamental optical properties. The refractive index describes how light travels through a material, while the extinction coefficient indicates how strongly the material absorbs it. Engineers need both measurements to predict how light will behave inside a waveguide, a structure designed to direct light along a specific path, and how much of the optical signal may be lost.

Getting consistent measurements from BTO has been surprisingly challenging. The material can contain multiple microscopic regions, called domains, in which the crystal structure points in different directions. Because these regions interact with light differently, measurements of an entire sample can combine several distinct responses. This has contributed to widely conflicting reports of BTO's optical properties over many decades.

Solving a Decades-Old Mystery About Light

To overcome this problem, the researchers used a sophisticated measurement method known as Mueller matrix spectroscopic ellipsometry. The technique examines how the polarization of light changes when light reflects from or passes through a material, allowing scientists to investigate its optical behavior in detail.

Rather than relying on crystals containing a complicated mixture of differently oriented regions, the team studied two types of single-crystal samples with relatively consistent domain orientations. This approach helped minimize overlapping optical responses and allowed the researchers to identify the material's underlying properties more accurately.

Their measurements spanned wavelengths from 190 nanometers (nm) to 40 micrometers (μm), covering an exceptionally broad range of light from ultraviolet to far-infrared. Since a material's optical behavior changes with wavelength, the scientists divided the spectrum into three regions and applied a different analytical approach to each. This revealed how BTO's refractive index and light absorption depend on both wavelength and crystal orientation.

The researchers also investigated a particularly important range in which BTO allows nearly all incoming light to pass through. By combining ellipsometry with separate measurements of light transmission, they detected extremely low absorption, determining extinction coefficients of approximately 10-5 in the 2-10 μm wavelength range. These precise values will help engineers estimate how much light is lost as it travels through or remains confined within optical components.

In another advance, the team developed a way to predict the combined optical behavior of crystals containing multiple domains. Their method uses the orientations of those domains and the proportion of the crystal occupied by each to calculate the material's overall response to light.

Opening the Door to Faster Data Transmission and Quantum Technology

The results could make the development of future optical devices more predictable and efficient. With accurate information about BTO's behavior, engineers can model how light will travel through components of different shapes and dimensions before manufacturing them. They can also better estimate absorption losses, potentially reducing the need for repeated prototypes, costly redesigns, and extensive testing.

The potential benefits extend beyond conventional optical communications. BTO could also play an important role in devices that produce light at different wavelengths, as well as photonic circuits that use light to process quantum information. Such technologies depend on controlling light with exceptional precision.

"This study reveals the optical response of barium titanate, which had long remained unclear, and provides a reliable reference for how the material interacts with light," said Professor Min Seok Jang.

Jang also emphasized that the findings could contribute to optical communication devices capable of transmitting data faster while reducing light loss. The improved understanding of BTO may also support the development of quantum photonic technologies, where precise manipulation of light is essential.

The study was published online on October 20, 2026, in ACS Photonics. Jiwon Kang, a Ph.D. candidate in KAIST's School of Electrical Engineering, and Dr. Nina Hong of J.A. Woollam Co. served as co-first authors. Professors Min Seok Jang of KAIST and Harry A. Atwater of Caltech were the corresponding authors.

Funding was provided through the Culture, Sports and Tourism R&D Program administered by the Korea Creative Content Agency (KOCCA), with support from the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism; the Basic Science Research Program administered by the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF), with support from the Ministry of Education; the Ministry of Science and ICT; and the U.S. Air Force Office of Scientific Research (AFOSR).

#4315. Ford Has A Dedicated Battery Abuse Team. It Obsesses Over How Cells Fail

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Electric vehicle batteries live a harder life than the ones in your phone or laptop. They spend most of their time outdoors, deal with extreme heat and cold, and can take a beating from road debris and potholes.

That means for battery makers, engineering for durability is a priority right up there with energy density and charging speed. And to make sure its cells can handle the abuse of daily life as an EV, Ford has a team dedicated to understanding how batteries fail—and how to stop it.

“That team is 100% focused on battery abuse, design, and testing as a function,” Wesley Thibault, the global chief engineer of battery product development at Ford said last week during a media roundtable at the automaker’s new battery plant in Marshall, Michigan.

Ford is new to the EV battery business. Last week, it started cranking out lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery packs at BlueOval Battery Park Michigan, using technology licensed from China’s CATL, the world’s largest battery maker. The batteries will power the all-important Ford Fathom pickup, which the automaker says will enter production toward the end of next year and kick off a new generation of vastly better and more profitable EVs.

Despite the licensing deal, Ford officials said they were involved in developing the batteries from the outset, with a focus on durability.

The job is not as simple as it sounds. The battery abuse team isn’t tasked with destroying fully made cells and then finding ways to make them indestructible. Instead, Thibault said, it is involved in the design process from the start.

“They want to understand down to the physics level, how a cell fails and why, and when it does fail, how we can prevent it from creating harm to the occupants,” he said.

Quality operator at Ford's BlueOval Battery Park Michigan.

For example, the team measures how cells vent, a crucial process that keeps batteries from catching fire or damaging themselves when they overheat. When temperatures inside a cell get too high, the electrolyte, the liquid chemical that shuttles electrons between the anode and cathode, gets hot and releases gases.

If those gases stay trapped, they can cause short circuits or thermal runaway, so they need to escape in a controlled way. Thibault said his team can measure all of this analytically—using computer models—before the cells are validated.

Production adds another layer of scrutiny. At various stages, the materials inside the cell, as well as the finished cell itself, go through thousands of quality checks, Ford engineers said. Those include CT scans, X-ray machines, lasers, camera inspections, and AI systems.

For example, when the anode slurry is coated onto a copper foil, every millimeter is scanned by lasers for wrinkles and other anomalies. All employees have the ability to pause production if they spot any problems.In case of any issues, they quarantine the cells affected during a specific time period. Ford also claimed that impacted components can be traced all the way from production to the vehicle they end up in.

To be sure, not all of this is unique to Ford. Strict quality checks like these are common among major battery makers, who all aim to minimize scrap rates for costly batteries and maximize the amount of material that actually gets sold.

Ford engineer operating a winding machine, which brings together the anode and cathode, adding a separator in between.

Ford continuously tests the manufacturing process in other ways, too. Engineers said they intentionally feed damaged components and cells—which they call “red rabbits”—into the production machinery to confirm the quality systems catch them and are working as intended.

When cells are almost ready, they’re blasted with helium gas to check for leaks. Once a pack is assembled, it’s mounted on a hydraulic shaker that mimics thousands of miles and years of real-world road use. The shaker can twist, dive, squat, contort, yaw, and replicate the other movements of a car, putting the pack through everything it would see on the road.

Ford’s EV batteries have fared well, by and large. High-mileage Mach-Es with 100,000 or even 200,000 miles on the odometer show little range loss compared to their original capacity, according to data the company released this month.

On the other hand, Ford’s emphasis on battery quality isn’t exactly surprising. The company has grappled with high warranty costs in recent years. And both the Mustang Mach-E and the F-150 Lightning have had issues linked to their high-voltage batteries. Some early Mach-Es were recalled because their battery contactors would overheat during DC fast-charging. A small number of Lightnings were recalled in 2023 due to defective battery cells.

Ford will want to avoid any similar quality issues as it rolls out the high-stakes Fathom, which it hopes will outsell its previous EVs and set the stage for an electric comeback. It will be years before we know how the Fathom's batteries hold up in the real world. For now, it looks like the company is pulling out all the stops to make sure things go off without a hitch.

#4313. One of the world’s biggest zinc mines is getting Alaska’s largest solar farm

Red Dog Mine in Alaska burns about 40,000 gallons of diesel a day to keep one of the world’s largest zinc mines running, and now, an 8.8-megawatt (MW) solar farm and battery storage will help cut that fuel use.

The Alaska Energy Authority’s board unanimously approved a nearly $5 million loan for the project through its Power Project Fund. Tugliq Red Dog1 will build, own, and operate the roughly $35 million solar project and sell the electricity to mine operator Teck Alaska. The state’s loan review says site work began in June and expects the solar and storage to come online in October 2028.

Red Dog sits about 105 miles north of the Arctic Circle, on land owned by NANA, an Iñupiat-owned Alaska Native corporation. The array would be larger than any solar farm operating in Alaska today, as KOTZ’s Desiree Hagen reported for Alaska Public Media. Hagen reported that the plans call for more than 15,000 panels across around 30 acres.

The mine gets all its power from on-site diesel generators. In summer, it can draw so much electricity that Teck has to cut power elsewhere at the site. The solar array and the 8.8 MW, 15 megawatt-hour (MWh) battery will give the operator another source of power during those crunches.

The state of Alaska expects the solar and storage project to cover about 5% of the zinc mine’s electricity needs under its current operating plan. The project could do even more after mining ends, covering about 90% of the site’s annual electricity needs.

Cost to import sun to a remote Alaskan village 0, cost to import diesel quite high.

A 500W panel weighs 60 lbs about the same as 9 gallons of diesel. 500W panel generates 750kwh of electricity a year each and every year for 20 years. 9 gallons of diesel gives you 350kwh of thermal energy which yields varying amounts of desired output.

Teck expects the mine’s existing deposits to support operations through 2031, and it’s studying whether to develop two nearby deposits. If that expansion goes ahead, the state projects the solar and battery project would cover about 3% of the larger operation’s electricity needs. If mining ends, demand will drop sharply, but the site will still need electricity for cleanup and long-term water treatment.

#4312. Scientists discover a hidden eye disease that slowly steals night vision

A newly identified genetic eye disease can gradually interfere with night vision and the ability to see objects at the edges of the visual field. The condition may be especially difficult to recognize because people can maintain good eyesight for much of their lives before noticeable problems develop.

An international research team, including scientists at the Scheie Eye Institute within the University of Pennsylvania's Perelman School of Medicine, traced the condition to a gene already associated with another form of vision loss. However, the two diseases affect eyesight in strikingly different ways. The previously known disorder primarily damages central vision, while the newly discovered condition affects peripheral vision and the ability to see in darkness.

Although the condition has not yet received an official name, researchers are calling it EFEMP1-associated late-onset retinal degeneration (L-ORD). It is linked to a specific genetic variant known as p.Arg140Trp in the EFEMP1 gene. This change causes an unusually thick accumulation of material between cells in the eye.

A Genetic Discovery That Began Decades Ago

The investigation traces back to 1998, when doctors documented an unusual pattern of vision loss in a family in the United States. As researchers uncovered new genetic evidence, they were able to connect those findings to families in Europe who showed similar symptoms.

The study, published in JAMA Ophthalmology, examined three unrelated families from different countries who carried the p.Arg140Trp variant. Their symptoms were compared with those of another family carrying a different change in the same gene, called p.Arg345Trp, which is associated with the previously recognized disease affecting central vision.

The international collaboration included researchers from Penn Medicine, the University of Edinburgh, the University of Basel, Charles University, and the University of Bonn.

At first, scientists suspected that the unusual symptoms in the original family might be caused by a different genetic disorder. Testing, however, failed to identify the variants responsible for that condition.

"The different disease expression in this family was thought to be similar to a condition caused by C1QTNF5 gene variants. However, none of the variants associated with that disease were found," said Artur V. Cideciyan, PhD, an ophthalmology researcher and co-director of the Center for Hereditary Retinal Degenerations. "Our collaborators then discovered a new variant in the EFEMP1 gene that normally causes a different disease where the macula, which is tied to central vision, is affected first."

How the New Eye Disease Affects Night Vision

The researchers found that the newly identified condition develops gradually in the outer regions of the retina. Located at the back of the eye, the retina detects incoming light and transforms it into signals that the brain uses to create visual images.

Unlike the previously known EFEMP1 disorder, which initially affects the macula and central vision, this newly identified disease begins in the peripheral retina. People may see normally for much of their lives before gradually noticing that their side vision is narrowing or that seeing in dim surroundings has become more difficult.

Problems may be particularly noticeable around dusk or at night, when the eyes must rely more heavily on specialized light-sensitive cells called rods.

One reason the disease is challenging to diagnose is that these cells may initially show no visible structural damage. The gradual progression of symptoms can make the condition even harder to recognize.

However, the researchers identified a potentially valuable early clue. In affected individuals, rod cells take unusually long to recover when the eyes move from bright surroundings into darkness. This abnormal response can be detected even when the retina still appears structurally normal.

"We can detect a major abnormality in the way rod photoreceptors recover in darkness with retinas that still look structurally intact," Cideciyan said. "This gives us a functional marker of disease at a stage when photoreceptor cells have not yet been lost."

The finding suggests that changes in how the retina functions may reveal the disease before the light-sensitive cells responsible for vision begin to disappear.

What the Discovery Could Mean for Age-Related Vision Loss

An important question remains unanswered: How many people carry this newly identified genetic variant?

Researchers suspect the condition is relatively uncommon, but they do not yet have enough information to determine its prevalence. Larger investigations will be necessary to establish how frequently the variant occurs and how many people may be affected.

Beyond identifying another inherited eye disorder, the findings could help scientists better understand why vision deteriorates with age. Studying rare genetic diseases can reveal biological processes that may also contribute to much more widespread retinal conditions.

"Aging is a risk factor for many medical conditions, including retinal diseases such as age-related macular degeneration, the most common retinal condition of aging," said Tomas S. Aleman, MD, a professor of ophthalmology and the other co-director of the Center for Hereditary Retinal Degenerations. "Lessons learned from these infrequent, late-onset genetic eye diseases offer glimpses at possible mechanisms of disease for much more frequent retinal problems."

By revealing how different changes in a single gene can produce distinct patterns of vision loss, the research adds to scientists' understanding of inherited retinal disease. It also highlights the potential importance of detecting changes in visual function before damage becomes apparent in the retina's structure.

The study received support from the University of Edinburgh Chancellor's Fellowship award, RS Macdonald Charitable Trust Seedcorn Award, the BrightFocus Foundation (M2024009N), the German Research Foundation (532367710), the Medical Research Council (MC_UU_00035/9, MC_UU_00007/10), the Swiss National Science Foundation (204285), the Ministry of Health of the Czech Republic (NW24-06-00083), Charles University in Prague (UNCE/24/MED/022 and SVV 2600631), and the Samuel G. Jacobson, MD, PhD, Memorial Fund.

#4311. VW’s Cheap EVs Are So Popular, Buyers Face Wait Times Of Nearly Two Years

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Volkswagen, along with its group siblings, Skoda and Seat, are facing huge demand for their small electric cars, which in turn is leading to wait times that are nearing two years in some cases.

With over 50,000 orders on tap already, the Volkswagen ID. Polo hatchback is one of the most successful models from the Volkswagen Group’s new Electric Urban Car Family, with the most affordable trim having wait times of up to 21 months in Germany, according to Spanish outlet Motor.es. That’s double compared to the 10-month wait times reported earlier this year.

Cupra Raval and Volkswagen ID. Polo production in Martorell, Spain

It’s a similar story when it comes to the technically similar Skoda Epiq, with over 80,000 orders since its introduction and wait times of up to 17 months for the most popular versions. The Cupra Raval, meanwhile, has amassed roughly 50,000 orders and has faced a multi-day production halt at the Martorell plant in Spain, where it shares an assembly line with the ID. Polo.

Together, the four models that make up the group’s affordable EV family, namely the Volkswagen ID. Polo, the Cupra Raval, the Skoda Epiq, and the Volkswagen ID. Cross, have attracted approximately 150,000 orders in Europe since their debut through the end of September.

It’s worth noting that while the cheap trims of all these cars, which start at around €24,995 ($27,300) in Germany, have put the Volkswagen Group in an unfavorable position, the more expensive versions are scheduled to ship a lot faster. The ID. Polo Sportline currently has a five-month wait time, while customers of the ID. Polo GTI have to wait roughly seven months.

The higher-than-expected demand has put all automakers at the mercy of battery cell suppliers. Currently, the Martorell factory that assembles the ID. Polo and Cupra Raval is working double shifts and has a daily output of up to 1,000 vehicles, but work has already begun to add a third shift, which would increase output to 1,200 vehicles daily.

The expansion is tied to battery production, and while there’s a factory nearby that can build up to 1,200 packs per day, it relies on cells that come from an external supplier. The same goes for the Pamplona plant that assembles the Volkswagen ID. Cross and Skoda Epiq electric crossovers. The two EVs share the same assembly line as VW’s combustion-powered T-Cross and Taigo, both of which bring in more money than their battery-powered counterparts.

A Volkswagen spokesperson told Germany's Automobilwoche that demand has increased “significantly more dynamically than originally expected” and that ramping up production “cannot be adjusted short-term to the same extent as this dynamically increasing demand.”

More employees are being added to the workforce, and Gotion’s new cell factory in Spain is expected to be fully operational early next year, which should help the automaker boost production without relying on outside help.

#4310. The e-bike industry has a horsepower problem

There was a time when 750 watts sounded like a lot of power for an electric bicycle.

These days, apparently those are rookie numbers.

Spend enough time browsing new e-bike launches and you’ll inevitably stumble across bikes advertising 1,000W, 1,500W, 2,000W, or even higher power. Dual-motor models have turned the spec sheet into an arms race, with manufacturers seemingly competing to see who can slap the biggest number onto the product page.

If you ask me, the e-bike industry is developing a horsepower problem.

To be clear, I’m not anti-power. I’ve ridden everything from dainty 250W European commuter bikes to electric motorcycles with enough power to rearrange your chest cavity. Powerful electric two-wheelers are fun, period.

But there’s a difference between building a powerful electric two-wheeler and pretending that every powerful electric two-wheeler is still an electric bicycle.

In the US, the widely adopted three-class e-bike system generally tops out at 20 mph (32 km/h) for Class 1 and Class 2 e-bikes and 28 mph (45 km/h) for Class 3, with some minor exceptions, and 750 watts has long been a common benchmark for the motor power limit.

Yet browse online e-bike retailers today and you’ll find plenty of machines advertised with motors well beyond that figure, often capable of speeds far beyond normal electric bicycle classifications.

Sometimes there’s a disclaimer explaining that the bike is intended for “off-road use.” Sometimes there’s a software setting that supposedly limits it for street riding.

And sometimes people just sort of squint at the pedals and agree to keep calling it an electric bicycle.

The problem isn’t that 2,000W electric two-wheelers exist. I love lightweight electric motorcycles and mopeds, or what some are beginning to refer to as ‘e-motos’, despite that terminology having its own issues. So sure, those bikes are great and there is a time and place for such power. The problem is that the industry increasingly seems afraid to call them what they are.

Part of the blame belongs to consumers – to us.

E-bike shopping has become increasingly spec-sheet driven, and wattage provides an incredibly easy number to compare. If ‘Bike A’ has a 750W motor and ‘Bike B’ costs the same but advertises 1,500W, it’s easy to assume ‘Bike B’ is twice as good. This is especially true for younger riders who lack a deeper understanding of how e-bikes work, and just want something powerful and fast to impress their friends after school. They beg their parents for the latest models with the biggest motors, and many parents give in.

The problem is that’s not how electric bikes work – there’s so much more to a bike than the motor wattage rating.

Motor design, controller current, battery voltage, thermal management, gearing, efficiency and software tuning all influence performance. A beautifully tuned 500W or 750W system can be far nicer to ride – and sometimes more useful – than a poorly implemented motor advertising twice the power.

But “excellent controller tuning” doesn’t look nearly as exciting in a giant font on an Amazon listing. So manufacturers respond rationally based on what consumers demand: They make the number bigger.

The result is an e-bike horsepower war that is ultimately hurting the entire industry.

When riders blast through bike paths on motorcycle-performance machines marketed as “e-bikes,” pedestrians don’t care whether the motor technically arrived in a street-legal mode. Police officers aren’t going to inspect controller settings. And lawmakers aren’t famous for approaching emerging transportation technology with surgical precision.

They see a fast machine with pedals, hear complaints about dangerous “e-bikes,” and start writing laws that affect everyone – including riders on perfectly ordinary commuter e-bikes.

In my opinion, that’s the part that should worry anyone who enjoys riding an e-bike.

In Germany cops inspect controller settings on e-bikes and scooters all the time and also do practical tests - they just get on the bike/scooter and manually test what max speed can it reach. If it exceeds the legal limit and does not carry the required paperwork for that - it gets confiscated on the spot at whoever drove it gets a fine and points on their license (even if they don't have one yet)

There’s absolutely a place for high-powered electric two-wheelers. In fact, I want more of them. Lightweight electric mopeds and motorcycles could replace an enormous number of car trips while using a fraction of the energy and space. Those are highly capable machines, but they need to be used appropriately, registered legally, and ridden responsibly.

And we don’t help that cause by pretending they’re bicycles.

Perhaps the e-bike industry’s next great innovation doesn’t need another 500 watts.

Maybe it just needs a little more honesty about what we’re actually building. So let’s build more electric bicycles. And yes, let’s build more e-motos and electric motorcycles. But let’s not confuse the two, either.

#4309. Driven: 2028 Porsche 718 Boxster EV Prototype Wags Its Tail Like a Mid-Engine Sports Car

The Boxster’s rear-biased weight distribution, which is unusual for an EV, makes it handle like a sports car should.

There’s still a lot that Porsche won’t divulge about its forthcoming 2028 718 Boxster EV, including horsepower, battery capacity, range, pricing, or even its final, un-camouflaged looks. But after some seat time around the handling course at the Porsche Experience Center Los Angeles, we now know what it feels like at—and a little bit beyond—its cornering limits.

Whether you’re welcoming the Boxster’s EV transition or bemoaning the loss of its internal-combustion engines, particularly the iconic flat-six, we think anyone who drives the next-generation 983 Boxster will agree it’s fantastic. The steering, inherited from the 992.2 911 Carrera GTS, is eager and sharp, and rear-axle steering will also be available. You can feel the Boxster’s rear-biased weight distribution in the way its rear end steps out when lifting off the throttle.

In other words, this new EV feels like a mid-engine Boxster, because that’s where the weight is concentrated. Other than some hypercars, such as the Rimac Nevera, the forthcoming electric Boxster rides atop one of the first EV platforms built around a two-seat sports car. The 800-volt battery pack lives entirely behind the passenger cabin, in the place the engine used to reside, which leads to a 40/60 front/rear weight distribution, similar to the gas-powered Boxster’s 45/55 split. And since there’s no battery under the floor, you sit as low as you would in any other sports car.

See all results for new 2028 Porsche 718 EV for sale near 78232

We drove what will become the top Boxster model when it goes on sale after its formal debut in early 2027, but Porsche wouldn’t confirm what it will be called. S? GTS? These models wear Pirelli P Zero R Elect tires—and for the first time—mount on staggered-diameter wheels just like the latest 911. The tires measure 255/35ZR-20 up front and 305/30ZR-21 in back, which is more meat than even the last 718 Spyder RS. The company isn’t saying how much power this Boxster’s single rear motor will make—all electric Boxsters will be rear-drive only—but they do claim the sprint to 60 mph will require less than 3.0 seconds. After experiencing being pinned to the seat by a few launch-control starts, the new Boxster feels every bit that quick.

Porsche says this will be the quickest, most powerful Boxster with the highest cornering and braking performance, with a center of gravity that’s—no surprise—much lower than before. We can attest to feeling tons of grip, but can we feel the EV’s added weight? As the Boxster slithered through transitions and dove into apexes, we can’t say it felt heavy, although the squealing from its wide tires sounded at times more tortured than those we recall from the just-over-3000-pound gas-powered Boxster. Porsche says the Boxster EV’s curb weight will fall somewhere within that of the 911 lineup, which ranges from the 3350-pound Carrera to the 4000-pound Turbo S Cabriolet. Here’s hoping it’s toward the lower end of that range, which would be very light for an EV.

See all results for new 2028 Porsche 718 EV for sale near 78232

While this new electric version looks like a Boxster and the low seating position feels like a Boxster, with a forward view of a quickly disappearing hood, Porsche wanted to add some more nostalgic tie-ins by way of fabricated engine noises and simulated shifts. The Taycan got a similar E-Shift feature earlier this year, but while the Taycan’s engine noises weren’t modeled after a specific engine, the Boxster’s very much pays homage to its past. The Boxster’s E-Shift, which is controlled by a knob on the steering wheel and can shift automatically or be controlled by steering wheel paddles, mimics the 981 Boxster GTS’s 3.4-liter flat-six, which Porsche engineers say is the high-water mark for flat-six wails. They told us emissions compromises to the most recent flat-sixes made them choose that one from circa 2015. That said, there’s a bit of revisionist history going on with the electric Boxster’s 8000-rpm “redline” versus the actual 7600-rpm redline in its 981 muse. Either way, the noise emanating from the two speakers—one inside the cabin, one outside—absolutely sounds like a flat-six.

Although the synthesized sound is a solid re-creation, we do think it would be easy to identify the real from the facsimile in a blindfolded test. There’s a lot of nuance going on in the sounds of a flat-six belting to redline—intake and exhaust noise, valve and other mechanical clatter—and it’s hard to generate all of that from a couple speakers. That said, after doing a few hot laps with the system on, we believe it adds to the experience, and it felt weird to switch over to silent and shift-free lapping. We think we’d use this more in a sports car like the Boxster than in the four-door Taycan sedan.

What else did we learn? As before, the 983 Boxster has both front and rear trunks, and its NACS charge port, which is hidden behind a powered door in the middle of the rear bumper, is the first from Porsche to accommodate both AC and DC charging. Today’s Cayenne and Taycan electrics have separate ports for AC and DC with the NACS only handling DC charging.

Officially, there won’t be any gas-powered Boxster variants, but who knows what the lifecycle might hold, especially if early sales disappoint. After all, remember when the previous generation went four-cylinder only, but then the flat-six made a reappearance a few years later? While we’re as sad as anyone to see the flat-six and manual transmission leave the Boxster lineup, we think that anyone who drives the new one will agree it’s a great-handling sports car.

#4308. A common blood pressure drug has a surprising effect on calorie-burning brown fat

A widely used blood pressure medication may have an unexpected benefit beyond its ability to control hypertension. Scientists have found that losartan can activate brown fat, a specialized type of body fat that burns energy, and improve metabolic activity in mice. The discovery suggests that an existing medication could potentially be repurposed to stimulate brown fat and support metabolic health.

Losartan belongs to a class of medications called angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB), which have an established safety profile. In a new study published in Nature, researchers found that the drug increased brown fat activity through a biological mechanism separate from its blood pressure effects. This raises the possibility of developing treatments that activate brown fat without lowering blood pressure.

The findings also revealed a surprising connection between brown fat and mental health. After examining data from more than 100,000 patients, researchers discovered that people with detectable brown fat had lower rates of several medical conditions, including anxiety and depression. This is the first time the research team has reported associations between brown fat and psychiatric health, adding to earlier evidence linking the tissue to better cardiovascular and metabolic health.

The research was led by Paul Cohen at Rockefeller University's Laboratory of Molecular Metabolism, working with Heiko Schöder and Daniel Lafontaine from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC). It expands on research published in 2021, when Cohen's team analyzed approximately 50,000 patients and found that those with more brown fat had substantially lower odds of developing cardiometabolic conditions such as coronary artery disease and type II diabetes.

"We only looked for a few diagnostic codes in that study, mainly focusing on cardiovascular disease since that's what this tissue has historically been associated with," says Cohen. "The scope of this new analysis is far more expansive. We doubled our number of patients and considered more than 500 codes, which allowed us to unearth many new insights."

AI Analysis Reveals New Benefits of Brown Fat

To investigate brown fat's relationship with human health, the researchers examined PET/CT scans from more than 100,000 patients who had undergone imaging as part of their cancer monitoring. They focused on scans showing brown adipose tissue, which can be found in six regions of the body, including the neck, armpits, and areas around organs such as the heart and kidneys.

The team used an approach known as reverse translation, which begins with observations in patients and then investigates the biological processes responsible for them. Cohen's laboratory has previously used this strategy to uncover important details about brown fat and its effects on health.

Nicolás Gómez-Banoy, the study's first author and an endocrinologist and instructor in clinical investigation in Cohen's laboratory, used a machine learning system developed by researchers at MSKCC to measure brown fat activity. The technology allowed him to assess both the total activity in each patient and the activity within each of the six anatomical regions.

The analysis showed that brown fat's location could be just as important as its presence. Activity in particular regions appeared to have stronger associations with certain health conditions, suggesting that brown fat may influence the body differently depending on where it is found.

"For example, the axillary, or armpit, area was linked to a decreased risk of high blood pressure compared to other regions," he says. "But overall, patients with brown fat have better glycemic parameters, lipid profiles, and echocardiographic indices, as well as lower inflammatory markers."

These findings indicate that people with brown fat tend to have healthier blood sugar levels, blood fat profiles, measures of heart function, and indicators of inflammation.

Common Blood Pressure Drug Activates Brown Fat

As the researchers investigated medications associated with brown fat activity, they noticed an intriguing pattern. Patients taking angiotensin receptor blockers were more likely to have detectable brown fat on their scans, suggesting that these widely prescribed medications might influence the tissue.

To explore that possibility, the team conducted laboratory experiments using cultured brown fat cells. They found that losartan directly increased the cells' metabolic activity, providing evidence that the drug could stimulate brown fat rather than simply being associated with its presence.

Even more interestingly, the researchers discovered that losartan activated brown fat through molecular pathways different from those responsible for lowering blood pressure. That distinction could be especially valuable for developing future medications that target metabolism without interfering with normal blood pressure regulation.

"The fact that its different effects are mediated by different molecular pathways is advantageous, since it means we could potentially isolate them in future therapies," says Gómez-Banoy. "That way you would be able to stimulate brown fat in people with normal blood pressure."

Additional experiments in healthy mice strengthened the findings. Animals given losartan showed increased energy expenditure, consumed more oxygen, and produced more carbon dioxide, all signs of heightened metabolic activity. Despite these changes, their body weight remained stable.

Brown Fat's Surprising Connection to Mental Health

Beyond its metabolic effects, brown fat may have a previously unrecognized relationship with psychological well-being. The patient analysis revealed that individuals with detectable brown fat had lower rates of anxiety and depression, extending the tissue's potential health associations beyond the cardiovascular system.

"We know that metabolically healthy people tend to have lower incidence of psychiatric diseases, so it could be that having brown fat makes you more metabolically healthy, and this correlates with fewer psychiatric issues," says Gómez-Banoy.

The researchers also found an intriguing relationship involving selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs, medications commonly prescribed to treat depression. These drugs appeared to suppress brown fat activity, suggesting another possible connection between psychiatric treatments and metabolic regulation.

However, the findings do not suggest that brown fat is beneficial in every respect. The analysis also identified higher rates of osteoporosis and certain skin diseases among people with brown fat, raising questions about possible trade-offs that require further investigation.

The discoveries have opened several avenues for future research. Scientists hope to examine the genetics of people with particularly high brown fat activity, investigate why the tissue is associated with lower rates of anxiety and depression, and determine whether its apparent benefits can be harnessed safely.

Losartan may also be only one of several existing medications worth investigating. The extensive patient analysis identified additional drugs associated with brown fat activity, offering researchers a range of potential candidates for future studies.

"There were plenty of other medications associated with brown fat activity in our large cohort," Cohen notes. "This is just a start."

Materials provided by Rockefeller University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
